title: Choose NOVAC's visual direction
question: Which direction should guide the landing page and calculator? All keep NOVAC's UAE HVAC purpose and calculator features.

options.label: UAE Climate Atlas
options.lineage: UAE climate atlases and municipal planning maps
options.thesis: Local design conditions lead, with every load traceable to its emirate and code basis.
options.viewport: A calm project header, selected emirate and design conditions, then familiar calculation sections.
options.risk: Map cues must stay subtle so the engineering inputs remain the focus.

raised.raise: A disciplined visible grid ties local conditions, charts and input groups together.

options.label: Urbanist Dashboard
options.thesis: A familiar, soft dashboard makes a complex engineering worksheet feel approachable.
options.viewport: Landing promise and live example lead into a modular project and load workspace.
options.risk: A familiar dashboard can feel generic unless UAE climate data stays visible.

options.label: Construction Grid
options.thesis: A measured grid makes the engineering worksheet feel precise and intentional.
options.viewport: Project inputs align to a quiet cell grid; charts and tables share its rhythm.
options.case: Strong precision signal, but weaker UAE-local recognition than the atlas.
options.risk: A visible grid can become visual noise if it competes with form fields.

options.label: Climate Timetable
options.thesis: A strict table rhythm makes design states and room schedules easy to compare.
options.viewport: The room schedule leads, with each design condition set in a fixed comparison column.
options.case: A timetable helps schedule scanning but is too narrow for the full calculator workflow.
options.kept: Dense tables should remain aligned and easy to scan.
options.risk: Angled panels and one-size typography would make engineering forms harder to read.

options.label: Coded Climate Index
options.thesis: Color-coded markers give every climate state a compact signature.
options.viewport: A climate-condition key labels the states used throughout the calculation.
options.case: A strong state key, but coded navigation reduces clarity for unfamiliar standards.
options.kept: Give each plotted climate state a consistent color and readable label.
options.risk: Encoded color cannot replace explicit engineering labels.

options.label: Climate Story Feed
options.thesis: One result at a time fills the screen for focused review.
options.viewport: A single room result fills the screen with a vertical next-room gesture.
options.case: The single-item sequence conflicts with simultaneous room comparison and form entry.
options.kept: Use clear focus states for the currently selected room.
options.risk: Hidden adjacent data slows engineering work.

options.label: Climate Data Tiles
options.thesis: Large color fields make key climate values visible at a glance.
options.viewport: Climate and load summary values lead in a tile panorama.
options.case: Color is memorable, but tile-only navigation weakens explicit workflow wayfinding.
options.kept: Use restrained color blocks to surface primary load results.
options.risk: Cropped display type can obscure long technical labels.

options.label: Variable Type Specimen
options.thesis: Typography shifts live to make hierarchy feel tactile.
options.viewport: A specimen-style headline sits above a compact load summary and controls.
options.case: A type axis is expressive but does not improve the calculation workflow.
options.kept: Keep data labels and values distinct through a clear type scale.
options.risk: A live type control would distract from engineering decisions.

canonCard.label: The standard calculator
canonCard.thesis: A familiar dashboard, executed with polished spacing and readable data.
canonCard.viewport: A conventional project form above a room list and load schedule.
canonCard.risk: Reliable, but visually less distinct from other calculators.
